This article introduces a five-dimensional framework—workload, state object, storage hierarchy, data movement and service objective—and a joint capacity, bandwidth, latency and energy model for token generation. Prefill and decoding differ in arithmetic intensity, state lifetime and objectives, making a single optimal hardware configuration unlikely. Low-bit microscaling, KV compression and sparse retention reduce bytes, but their gains depend on conversion, accuracy recovery and reversibility. Disaggregation, global KV caches, CXL pools and near-memory compute elevate KV from device-local temporary data to independently schedulable state. Efficient architectures should combine value-aware placement, reversible compression, communication/computation overlap and heterogeneous chiplets, rather than merely add matrix units. Capacity examples, a token Roofline method and reproducible metrics support joint chip, compiler and serving-system design.
